title: In re National Football League Players Concussion Injury Litigation (final approval)
lead: Retired football players and the NFL revised a proposed concussion settlement until an uncapped compensation program and separate representation could support final class approval.

actors.name: Retired professional football players and their families
National Football League
actors.role: Defendant settling without an admission of liability

actors.name: Kevin Turner and Shawn Wooden
actors.role: Representatives of diagnosed and undiagnosed subclasses

actors.name: Judge Anita B. Brody
actors.role: District judge overseeing the multidistrict litigation

proceedings: 2013: discovery stayed while preemption motion was briefed; court ordered mediation.
January 2014: preliminary approval denied for capped proposal.
July 2014: revised settlement received preliminary approval; notice and November hearing followed.
April 22, 2015: class and subclasses certified, amended settlement approved, and final judgment entered.
limits: This is the district court’s 2015 approval, distinct from the 2014 refusal and 2016 appellate affirmance. Scientific descriptions are the 2015 settlement record, not current medical findings. Separately incorporated settlement exhibits are not represented as separately reviewed.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Former players challenge the league’s handling of head injuries
sections.cue: Introduce the alleged wrong and the unresolved litigation risks.
paragraphs: Retired professional football players alleged that the National Football League, or NFL, knew of long-term neurological dangers from repeated head impacts but concealed information and failed to protect them. Their state-law theories included negligence and fraud. Players reported dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, and other symptoms; survivors relied in part on postmortem diagnoses of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE. None of these allegations became an adjudication of the league’s tort liability in the settlement decision.

The first concussion suit identified in the opinion was filed by seventy-three players in California on July 19, 2011, followed by others including Easterling. By settlement, the multidistrict litigation included more than 300 lawsuits and approximately 5,000 players. Claims against helmet manufacturer Riddell remained separate.

The NFL argued that collective bargaining agreements preempted the claims under § 301 of the Labor Management Relations Act. District Judge Anita B. Brody stayed discovery, received extensive briefing, and heard argument in April 2013. She did not decide the motion before settlement, leaving preemption a substantial risk rather than an established defense.

sections.title: A capped proposal fails and negotiations continue
paragraphs: Brody ordered mediation in July 2013 under retired Judge Layn Phillips. Counsel used medical experts, legal analysis, and a database of impaired plaintiffs while negotiating a $765 million proposal. A financial special master was appointed in December 2013. In January 2014, Kevin Turner and Shawn Wooden filed the settlement-class complaint, but Brody refused preliminary approval. She questioned whether the capped monetary fund would last sixty-five years and raised concerns about the releases.

Further negotiations removed the monetary-award cap and narrowed releases. Preliminary approval followed in July 2014, then notice and a November fairness hearing. Brody required additional improvements incorporated in February 2015: credit for NFL Europe play, protection of baseline examinations despite that program’s cap, extension of the CTE-death cutoff to final approval, and better claims procedures.

At the April 2015 decision, the court reported 208 remaining opt-outs and 205 objectors joining eighty-three written objections. Those were this stage’s counts, distinct from the later appeal. The additional hearing and revisions also meant that final approval was a separate event from the negotiations immediately after the January 2014 refusal.

sections.title: The revised agreement covers present and future diagnoses
sections.cue: Describe the negotiated benefits and conditions.
paragraphs: The class covered retired NFL players, authorized representatives of deceased or incapacitated players, and derivative claimants. Independently represented subclasses divided those without qualifying diagnoses before preliminary approval from those already diagnosed, including specified deceased players. Turner had ALS; Wooden lacked a qualifying diagnosis. They represented the immediate-compensation and future-protection interests respectively.

An uncapped, inflation-adjusted monetary program would last sixty-five years. A qualifying player did not have to establish that NFL football caused the condition or prove individual tort damages. Scheduled maximum awards were $1.5 million for Level 1.5 neurocognitive impairment, $3 million for Level 2 impairment, $3.5 million each for Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s diseases, $4 million for death with CTE before final approval, and $5 million for ALS. Actual awards varied with age at diagnosis and credited seasons, and specified offsets applied. Worsening conditions could support supplemental awards.

A separate $75 million, ten-year baseline-assessment program offered examinations and some treatment for lesser impairment; it did not itself diagnose Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, or ALS. A $10 million fund supported education and prevention. Appropriately credentialed professionals’ diagnoses before the effective date were honored under specified rules; later diagnoses required approved providers and settlement criteria.

sections.title: The court examines representation before approving the compromise
paragraphs: Settlement did not reduce the requirements of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23. Approximately 20,000 retired players satisfied numerosity. Common questions concerned the NFL’s alleged withholding of information and failure to protect players. Different careers, symptoms, and awards did not remove that shared conduct. The court distinguished Wal-Mart, the Supreme Court case concerning decentralized employment decisions. Turner’s and Wooden’s theories were typical of their respective subclasses.

Brody found capable representatives, experienced counsel, sustained adversarial bargaining, and genuine separate representation. Named players did not have to negotiate every term themselves. Unlike a fixed fund that present claimants could exhaust, the uncapped program, inflation adjustment, and supplemental awards protected future claimants. Differences in amounts and offsets reflected severity, claim value, and litigation risks rather than fundamental antagonism. Wooden did not know which illness he might develop and had reason to seek broad protection. The court found no need to create a new subclass for every symptom or disease.

Shared questions about knowledge, conduct, and the scientific relationship to injury predominated over individual calculations. Brody distinguished Amchem, the Supreme Court’s asbestos settlement case involving a more heterogeneous population. One settlement was superior to decades of repetitive, uncertain litigation, and trial-management difficulties did not need assessment for a settlement-only class. These were case-specific conclusions reinforced by the mediator, special master, and continuing supervision.

sections.title: Notice and independent fairness review protect absent members
sections.cue: Describe what the court checked beyond counsel’s agreement.
paragraphs: Summary and long-form notices described the action, class, benefits, releases, hearing, objections, and opt-out consequences. More than 30,000 addresses drawn from thirty-three datasets supported individual mailings, supplemented by publication, a website, and telephone assistance. The notice expert estimated ninety-percent reach. Due process required reasonable methods, not proof of actual receipt by every member. The original notice used the then-current preliminary-approval CTE deadline. Later amendments only improved benefits without new concessions to the NFL, so the court did not require a new class-wide notice and opt-out period.

Applying the settlement factors from Girsh and Prudential, Brody independently considered complexity, expense, delay, reactions, available information, proof and certification risks, ability to pay, and possible recoveries. Counsel’s experience and arm’s-length bargaining supported an initial fairness presumption but did not replace examination. Medical and historical proof, causation, and preemption presented serious uncertainty; impaired players needed timely help. Informal investigation, experts, and the database supplied meaningful information despite stayed formal discovery. The NFL’s ability to pay was neutral because it had not claimed inability to pay more.

Fees were negotiated after substantive terms and would be paid separately. The NFL’s agreement not to oppose up to $112.5 million was not an award. Brody reserved the fee decision, objections, and a Rule 23(h) hearing, retaining power to reject unreasonable compensation.

sections.title: CTE objections require careful limits on the scientific account
sections.cue: Keep the negotiated coverage distinct from medical certainty.
paragraphs: Brody considered the scientific evidence available in 2015, including limited and selected postmortem samples and disputed causal inferences. Many cognitive symptoms associated with CTE could qualify for dementia-based awards without proving CTE. Excluding compensation solely for mood or behavioral symptoms reflected difficult causation and competing risk factors. An expert’s estimate that at least eighty-nine percent of subjects in examined studies would qualify did not establish that percentage for all retired players.

The special death-with-CTE benefit stopped at final approval. The court discussed avoiding a suicide incentive, but more importantly protecting families of deceased players who lacked adequate notice to obtain qualifying diagnoses. Living players could seek diagnoses and benefits for covered symptoms. Scientific developments would be discussed in good faith at ten-year intervals, but modification required agreement and judicial oversight; future coverage was not guaranteed.

The court reviewed diagnostic thresholds, age and season adjustments, and seventy-five-percent offsets for specified severe traumatic brain injury or stroke. Clear and convincing proof that the other injury did not cause the qualifying condition could overcome those offsets. The triggering severe injury differed from the repetitive mild injuries alleged in the suit.

sections.title: Administrative protections support the long-term program
sections.cue: Describe access, enforcement, and remaining reservations.
paragraphs: Registration ordinarily had to occur within 180 days after effectiveness notice, subject to good cause. Claims generally were due within two years of diagnosis or supplemental notice, whichever was later, with hardship protection. Medical and employment records were required, but the NFL had to supply missing employment information. Representatives and counsel could assist, deficient submissions could be corrected, and claims could be appealed. The $1,000 appeal fee was refundable after success and subject to hardship waiver. Monthly audits, independent administration, judicial supervision, qualified providers, standardized examinations, and stopping rules for impaired examinees addressed burden concerns. Registration was an administrative benefit requirement, not conversion of the class into an opt-in suit.

Releases covered head, brain, and cognitive injuries against NFL parties while preserving claims against the National Collegiate Athletic Association, amateur and youth organizations, and Riddell, as well as specified collective-bargaining and benefit rights. The education fund was a negotiated benefit rather than leftover cy pres money; alternatively, it related to football injury prevention.

Representatives of players who died before 2006 still had to establish timeliness under state law. Federal American Pipe class-action tolling did not itself govern those state claims; applicable state analogues required examination. Security, reserves, future trusts, continuing league obligations, remedies for material default, and lien administration supported payment without eliminating every risk. Paid experts were not presumptively biased, and objectors had no absolute right to discovery or public disclosure of all NFL information as a condition of settlement.

sections.title: The final order binds participating class members without finding liability
paragraphs: On April 22, 2015, Brody certified the class and subclasses under Rules 23(a) and 23(b)(3), approved the amended agreement under Rule 23(e), and entered final judgment. The appended order confirmed representatives and counsel, appointed administrators and joint special masters, incorporated the settlement documents, required performance, and preserved insurers’ policy obligations. It expressly disclaimed an admission of liability.

The order dismissed the class complaint and related pending suits with prejudice, excluded opt-outs from the binding settlement, reserved fee motions, and retained exclusive continuing enforcement jurisdiction. Later changes required court approval and written agreement of the parties’ counsel. No separate judicial opinion accompanied the decision. Approval established the acceptability of this compensation compromise and class structure; it did not establish the NFL’s underlying tort liability or decide the later appellate stage.
